blocks.text: The “living stones” and “spiritual house” describe a community gathered around Christ, the scriptural cornerstone, rather than a literal building, a clerical class, or a territorial state. The titles “royal priesthood” and “holy nation” draw on Israel’s scriptures; the letter reasons through those scriptures rather than erasing Israel or declaring Jewish people rejected.

The phrase translated “spiritual milk” can be understood as rational, spiritual, or word-related nourishment. The wording alone does not settle a sacramental meaning or set faith against intellectual reflection.

The readers are urged to answer slander with visible good works, but this need not mean assimilation, respectability politics, concealing abuse, or remaining silent about injustice. The letter attests hostility and suffering, yet it does not identify a particular emperor or an empire-wide persecution decree.

Submission to human authorities is framed alongside freedom, honoring everyone, love for fellow believers, fear of God, and honor for the king. Read within those limits, the paragraph is not a command for unlimited obedience or a justification for authoritarian rule or harmful commands.

Verses 18–20 address enslaved household members, including those under unjust masters; this is an exploitative status relation, not a benign description of employment. Christ’s suffering is then presented both as an example and through sin-bearing, wounds, healing, shepherd, and guardian imagery. That example cannot mean seeking harm, staying with an abuser, refusing rescue, or shielding perpetrators from accountability; later atonement theories add further interpretation beyond these images.

sections.title: Reading the Calls to Conduct and Submission

blocks.text: The suffering language in verses 21–25 recalls Isaiah 52:13–53:12, which portrays a servant’s humiliation, suffering, death, representative bearing, vindication, and benefit to others. Isaiah does not explicitly name the servant, and collective, individual, prophetic, messianic, and christological readings have long histories.

The “not a people” and mercy language in 2:9–10 reuses Lo-ammi and Lo-ruhamah language also used in Romans 9, but in distinct communities. Neither use authorizes contempt for Jews or antisemitism. More broadly, the letter’s language leaves the exact demographic makeup of its recipients—Jewish, gentile, or mixed—open to debate.
The letter’s language supports debate over whether its recipients were Jewish, gentile, or mixed; it does not settle their exact demographics.

This chapter belongs to a coherent letter that combines blessing, moral exhortation, interpretation of scripture, household instruction, and hope shaped by God’s future action. That wider pattern helps explain why communal identity, public conduct, authority, and suffering appear together here.
